source: Jones (2021) Scaling Scaling Laws with Board Games
finding: Older AI system (AlphaZero on Hex): train-time compute and test-time search compute trade off along a straight line in log-compute.
numbers: Each extra 10x of train compute lets you cut about 15x of test compute at equal strength, down to a floor of single-node tree search.
quote: for each additional 10x of train-time compute, about 15x of test-time compute can be eliminated
limits: Only Hex; the author says it may not hold in other games.
agent_relevance: Early evidence that test compute can substitute for model quality. Supports a per-problem budget, not a fixed one.

source: Cobbe et al. (2021) Training Verifiers to Solve Math Word Problems
finding: Sampling many solutions and picking one with a trained verifier beats plain fine-tuning on GSM8K; verifiers scale better with data.
numbers: Verifier gain is about the same as a 30x model size increase versus the fine-tuning baseline (GPT-3 6B and 175B, GSM8K).
limits: Needs a trained verifier; 2021 models; math only.
agent_relevance: Origin of best-of-N with a checker. Fits G5: a separate checker selects.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning
finding: Sample many reasoning paths at temperature and take the most common final answer.
numbers: Gains over greedy CoT: GSM8K +17.9, SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2, StrategyQA +6.4, ARC-challenge +3.9 points.
limits: Gains shrink on commonsense tasks; needs a short comparable final answer; votes from one model are correlated.
agent_relevance: Baseline parallel-compute method. Cheap and strong, but agreement is only a hint (G4).

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Coverage (fraction solved by any sample) rises log-linearly with number of samples over orders of magnitude, fit by an exponentiated power law.
numbers: CodeContests with Gemma-2B: 0.02% at 1 sample to 7.1% at 10,000 (over 300x). SWE-bench Lite, DeepSeek-Coder-V2: 15.9% at 1 sample to 56% at 250, above the single-sample SOTA of 43%.
quote: coverage growing nearly log-linearly with the number of samples over several orders of magnitude
limits: Coverage turns into accuracy only where an automatic verifier exists; without one, voting and reward models plateau.
agent_relevance: Supports many cheap draws when code can check them (G2, G3). Without a checker, extra samples help little.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally Can Be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: Best way to spend test compute depends on question difficulty. A difficulty-adaptive allocation ('compute-optimal') beats uniform spending.
numbers: Compute-optimal search beats best-of-N using up to 4x less test compute (MATH, PaLM-2, PRM search and revisions). FLOPs-matched against a 14x larger pretrained model: test compute wins on easy and medium questions.
quote: Test-time and pretraining compute are not 1-to-1 exchangeable
limits: On the hardest questions test compute gives little; pretraining is more effective. Beam search hurts on easy questions (levels 1-2) and helps on harder ones (levels 3-4). Easy questions prefer sequential revision; hard ones need a mix.
agent_relevance: Direct source for G12: budget by difficulty and search only with a foothold. Difficulty must be estimated cheaply.

source: Wu et al. (2025, ICLR) Inference Scaling Laws: An Empirical Analysis of Compute-Optimal Inference
finding: Smaller models with a better search algorithm (REBASE) are compute-optimal; larger models win only once small-model sampling saturates.
numbers: Llemma-7B with REBASE matches Llemma-34B accuracy at about 2x fewer FLOPs on MATH500 and GSM8K; 7B beats 34B until 128 samples are drawn; 7B+REBASE beats 34B+majority vote at all budgets.
limits: Math only; Llemma and Mistral families; PRM-based search.
agent_relevance: Supports spending on search with a small model instead of a bigger one, when a foothold exists.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Can 1B LLM Surpass 405B LLM? Rethinking Compute-Optimal Test-Time Scaling
finding: Best test-time strategy depends on policy model, reward model and difficulty; small models with the right strategy beat much larger ones.
numbers: Llama-3.2-1B with compute-optimal TTS beats Llama-3.1-405B on MATH-500; a 0.5B model beats GPT-4o and a 7B model beats o1 and DeepSeek-R1 on MATH-500 and AIME24 (as reported by the authors).
quote: a 1B LLM can exceed a 405B LLM on MATH-500
limits: Needs a good PRM; math only; the paper notes some 1B outputs lacked \boxed, so answer extraction was adjusted.
agent_relevance: Reinforces G12: adapt strategy per item. Verifier quality sets the ceiling.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling
finding: Fine-tune on 1,000 traces, then control thinking length with budget forcing (cut thinking off, or append 'Wait' to extend). Accuracy rises with thinking tokens.
numbers: s1-32B: AIME24 50% to 57% when extending with Wait; up to 27% over o1-preview on competition math (MATH, AIME24). Parallel majority voting on Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct (up to 64 draws) did not catch up with s1-32B.
quote: the methods we investigate eventually flatten out or further scaling fails due to control or context window limitations
limits: Scaling flattens, then fails due to control and context window limits. Training on all 59K examples did not beat the 1K selection. Traces distilled from a stronger teacher.
agent_relevance: A hard cap is controllable but returns flatten. Supports a cap per mode (G11) and few extensions.

source: Ji et al. (2025) A Survey of Test-Time Compute: From Intuitive Inference to Deliberate Reasoning
finding: Frames test-time compute from System-1 (adaptation, input change, output calibration) to System-2 (repeated sampling, self-correction, tree search).
numbers: Survey; no single headline number.
limits: Mostly summarises others; no matched-cost comparison across families.
agent_relevance: Map of the field; use it to locate methods, not as effect-size evidence.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: o1-like models spend huge token counts on trivial questions; most later solutions repeat the first correct one.
numbers: On '2+3' o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models. The first correct solution is only about 38.7% of tokens on ASDIV. Self-training cut tokens 48.6% on MATH500 with QwQ-32B-Preview at kept accuracy.
quote: o1-like models consumed 1,953% more tokens than conventional models
limits: QwQ-32B-Preview and R1-class models; the fix needs training, not a prompt.
agent_relevance: Strong case for an S0 gate: easy items should skip long thinking (G11, G12).

source: Zeng et al. (2025) Revisiting the Test-Time Scaling of o1-like Models
finding: Longer chains of thought in o1-like models do not reliably raise accuracy; correct answers tend to be shorter than wrong ones for the same question.
numbers: Across QwQ, R1-Distill and LIMO, all sizes and datasets: mean length of correct solutions below incorrect ones. Parallel scaling beats 40-step sequential self-revision on coverage (10 samples). Sequential revision helps R1-Distill-32B up to about 10k tokens then stops. Shortest Majority Vote beats plain majority vote on AIME and GPQA.
quote: correct solutions are often shorter than incorrect ones for the same questions
limits: Longer chains hold more self-revisions, which often hurt. Length is confounded with difficulty, partly handled by within-question comparison.
agent_relevance: Supports G11 (several short attempts beat one long) and a length-aware code selector (G5).

source: Hassid et al. (2025) Don't Overthink it: Preferring Shorter Thinking Chains for Improved LLM Reasoning
finding: Pick the shortest of several sampled chains (short-1@k). It matches or beats majority voting in low compute.
numbers: Shortest chain up to 34.5% more accurate than the longest for the same question; shortest chains are 50% and 67% shorter than random and longest; up to 40% fewer thinking tokens and up to 33% wall time reduction versus majority vote in low-compute settings.
limits: Reasoning models on math and reasoning sets; benefit fades at high sample counts.
agent_relevance: Independent confirmation of Zeng. Cheap rule for code to pick among attempts.

source: Zhao et al. (2025) Sample, Scrutinize and Scale: Effective Inference-Time Search by Scaling Verification
finding: Random sampling plus model self-verification scales; verifying more candidates also makes verification more accurate ('implicit scaling').
numbers: Gemini 1.5 Pro, Verification@200 vs Pass@1 vs o1-Preview: AIME 8/15 vs 1/15 vs 7/15; MATH 467/500 vs 426 vs 428; LiveBench Math 135/200 vs 104 vs 131; LiveBench Reasoning 97/140 vs 63 vs 95. Consistency@200 only 4/15 on AIME.
quote: frontier models demonstrate remarkably weak out-of-box verification capabilities
limits: Authors say frontier models have weak out-of-box verification; AIME has only 15 items so noise is large; o1-Preview re-measured at 26% not the reported 44% on AIME.
agent_relevance: Self-verification of many candidates beats plain voting but sits uneasily with G4 and G10 unless the check uses real output. Use with caution.

source: Setlur et al. (2025) Scaling Test-Time Compute Without Verification or RL is Suboptimal
finding: Theory and experiments: methods that train on expert traces without a verifier (distillation like s1) fall behind verifier-based RL or search as compute and data grow.
numbers: Proof of a widening gap when base-model correctness varies across problems; gap shown in practice as test-time tokens and data scale.
limits: Gap depends on heterogeneity of the base model.
agent_relevance: Argues a checker is what makes extra tokens useful. Fits G2 and G3.

source: Gema et al. (2025, TMLR) Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute
finding: Built tasks where longer reasoning lowers accuracy across large reasoning models. Five failure modes.
numbers: Models include Claude Sonnet 3.7/4, Opus 4, o3-mini, o4-mini, o3, Qwen3-32B, QwQ-32B, DeepSeek R1. Failure modes: Claude distracted by irrelevant info; o-series overfit framing; drift to spurious correlations; lost focus on deduction; Sonnet 4 shows more self-preservation talk in longer reasoning.
limits: Synthetic tasks built to show the effect; not a claim that all tasks invert.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition for G11: extra thinking can hurt with distractors, so cap it and use an S0 gate.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking
finding: On controllable puzzles, reasoning models show three regimes by complexity and then collapse.
numbers: Matched pairs Claude 3.7 Sonnet thinking vs not, and DeepSeek R1 vs V3 at equal tokens: at low complexity non-thinking is equal or better and cheaper; at medium complexity thinking wins; at high complexity both collapse to zero. Reasoning effort falls near the collapse point despite spare token budget.
limits: Challenged by Lawsen (next line): token limits and unsolvable instances.
agent_relevance: Supports a difficulty gate: thinking pays only in a middle band.

source: Lawsen (2025) The Illusion of the Illusion of Thinking
finding: Comment arguing the collapse is largely an artefact of output token limits, auto-grading and impossible instances.
numbers: Tower of Hanoi needs exponentially many moves so output limits are hit; River Crossing instances for N >= 6 were mathematically impossible; asking for a generating function gave high accuracy (preliminary, multiple models).
limits: Short comment with preliminary tests; no full benchmark rerun.
agent_relevance: Warns that apparent failure of long thinking can be a budget or grading artefact. Log truncation.

source: Ma et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Can Be Effective Without Thinking
finding: Skipping the thinking block (NoThinking) by prompt beats Thinking at matched tokens in low budgets; more samples close the gap.
numbers: With DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen: 51.3 vs 28.9 on AMC 23 at 700 tokens. NoThinking with N parallel samples and best-of-N matches Thinking at up to 9x longer latency.
limits: Advantage fades at high token budgets; distilled R1 models; seven datasets.
agent_relevance: Supports an S0 gate and G11: many short non-thinking attempts can beat one long chain at equal budget.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Do We Truly Need So Many Samples? Multi-LLM Repeated Sampling (ModelSwitch)
finding: Switch between models by consistency and stop sampling early. Beats self-consistency and debate at lower cost.
numbers: Saves 34% of samples on average over six datasets (up to 43% on GSM8K, 41% on MGSM) at budget 16. 63.2% on MMLU-Pro versus MAD 47.6%, AgentVerse 44.8%, MOA 52.6%; beats GPT-4o and Gemini 1.5 Pro using their smaller siblings.
limits: Needs several comparable models; agreement as a stop signal inherits correlated-error risk (G4).
agent_relevance: Gives a concrete adaptive-stop rule on agreement and supports G9 (no debate).

source: Yang et al. (2025) Dynamic Early Exit in Reasoning Models (DEER)
finding: Training-free: watch model confidence at reasoning-transition points and exit early when confident.
numbers: CoT length cut 19.1% to 80.1% on average while accuracy changes by +0.3% to +5.0% across AIME 2024, AMC 2023, MATH-500, GPQA Diamond and BigCodeBench.
limits: Uses model confidence; confidence may be miscalibrated.
agent_relevance: A cheap stop rule for S0 and budget caps, but confidence is not proof (G10).

source: Sui et al. (2025) Stop Overthinking: A Survey on Efficient Reasoning for Large Language Models
finding: Survey of ways to make reasoning efficient: shorten, compress or route by difficulty.
numbers: Survey; no single effect size.
limits: Reports numbers from other papers without re-testing.
agent_relevance: Catalogue of ways to enforce G11 and G12.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Sleep-time Compute: Beyond Inference Scaling at Test-time
finding: Pre-compute useful facts about the context before the question arrives; this lowers test-time cost.
numbers: Same accuracy with about 5x less test-time compute on Stateful GSM-Symbolic and Stateful AIME; scaling sleep-time compute adds up to 13% and 18% accuracy.
limits: Works only when the context is known ahead and queries are predictable; custom stateful benchmark versions.
agent_relevance: Option for using idle budget in memory building; not for single-shot problems.

source: Snell et al. (2024) section on search versus best-of-N by difficulty
finding: Stronger optimisation against a verifier hurts on easy questions and helps on hard ones.
numbers: Beam search degrades versus best-of-N on levels 1-2 of MATH; beats it on levels 3-4 (PaLM-2, PRM).
limits: Over-optimising an imperfect verifier on easy items is exploitable.
agent_relevance: Do not run search on easy items; reserve it for items with a foothold (G12).

source: Snell et al. (2024) sequential versus parallel split
finding: The best mix of sequential revision and parallel sampling depends on question difficulty.
numbers: Easy questions benefit most from purely sequential compute; harder questions have an ideal ratio of sequential to parallel (PaLM-2 revision model, MATH).
limits: Ratio tuned per difficulty bin from verifier estimates.
agent_relevance: Choose revise-vs-resample by difficulty estimate, not one fixed recipe.

source: Zeng et al. (2025) coverage of sequential versus parallel scaling
finding: At equal generated tokens, parallel sampling gives a clearly larger coverage gain than sequential self-revision for QwQ and R1-Distill-32B; majority vote needs at least 3 samples to help.
numbers: Sequential: 40 self-revision steps. Parallel: 10 samples. Sequential cost is higher because attention covers longer context.
limits: Coverage is an upper bound; selection still needed.
agent_relevance: Prefer several short independent attempts to one long chain (G11, S3 fresh context).
